title: The Levy and the Vihuela: Hernández, from the Perdriel Chacra to the Twelfth Edition
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Chacra de Perdriel, birth in the Pueyrredón house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The pin is the coordinate already carried for the Chacra de Perdriel in juan_martin_de_pueyrredon.journey.json; a present-day geocode of the Museo Histórico José Hernández at Pasaje 113, Villa Coronel José María Zapiola, partido de General San Martín, gives -34.56217, -58.57250, some three hundred metres off, and the research pool's own geography lens carried -34.538, -58.562, which is wrong by nearly three kilometres
stops.campa: In a room of the chacra his mother's family has held since before the century turned, Isabel de Pueyrredón gives birth to a son and he is called José Rafael. The ground outside is the ground where Juan Martín de Pueyrredón mustered criollo horsemen against the British in 1806 and was broken there in a single morning. The mother's people own this field and have owned it for two generations. The father, Rafael Hernández, is a mayordomo out on the southern frontier, working other men's cattle. He is not at the birth.
suggested_refs: The Chacra Pueyrredón at Perdriel, today the Museo Histórico José Hernández, partido de General San Martín
The Combate de Perdriel, 1 August 1806, fought on the same property

stops.name: La Merced, the baptism nine months late
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Spanish biography; the parish register itself was not consulted, and the identification of La Merced as the church is described in the source material as traditional
stops.campa: The child is carried into the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Merced on Reconquista street and baptized José Rafael Hernández, eight months and seventeen days after he was born. Biographers count the interval and none of them explains it. Rosas is governor. The church stands three blocks from the fort, in a city where the parish book is the only register of a birth there is. The countryside where the father works is a day's ride away and a whole political world away. The entry gives the day, the parents, and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Merced, Buenos Aires, July 1835
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Merced (Buenos Aires)'

stops.name: Barracas, the grandfather's house
stops.date_confidence: approximate and reconstructed: the episode rests on family biography, is tagged R in the research pool, and carries no date. The year orders the segment. The house is not located and the pin is the Barracas neighbourhood centre
stops.campa: The Pueyrredones are unitarios and Rosas is in power, so his mother's people cross the river to Montevideo. The boy does not go with them. He is left in Barracas with his father's father, José Gregorio Hernández Plata, in a federal household on the southern edge of the city. The whole episode comes down through the family and no document behind it has been found. Both languages of the quarrel that will run through everything he later writes are spoken over him before he can read either one. He is six.
suggested_refs: The Hernández Plata household in Barracas, Buenos Aires, under the Rosas government
sources: Research pool, family biographical tradition, tagged R

stops.name: San Telmo, the Liceo Argentino
stops.date_confidence: span, defaulted to the first year: the Spanish biography puts him at the Liceo between 1841 and 1845 without exact dates. The school's street address is not located and the pin is the San Telmo neighbourhood centre. The tradition that Pedro Sánchez waived his fees for merit is family testimony only and is not carried here
stops.campa: At Pedro Sánchez's Liceo Argentino in San Telmo he is taught letters, Christian doctrine, grammar, arithmetic, history and drawing, and later French and geometry. Four years. It is the whole of his formal education. Law, political economy, cattle management, stenography, the Spanish sentence: everything else he will need he teaches himself, mostly in newspaper offices. The schooling ends when his chest gives trouble and the doctors order him out of the city air.
suggested_refs: The Liceo Argentino of Pedro Sánchez, San Telmo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Laguna de los Padres, sent south for his chest
stops.date_confidence: span 1846 to 1852, defaulted to the first year and tagged R. The specific estates are not identified in any source reached; the pin is Laguna de los Padres, the nearest fixed landmark the sources name, in the Camarones zone of the southern frontier
stops.campa: The prescribed cure is the pampa. He is sent to his father on the southern frontier, where Rafael Hernández is mayordomo on estates tied to Juan Manuel de Rosas, He learns to ride, to work cattle, and to sleep on the ground. He learns the levy, the justice of the peace, the fort that swallows a gaucho for a season and does not give him back, and the speech of men who own nothing at all. He is twelve years old, and he will live out here for six years. Not one day of them is dated in any source reached.
suggested_refs: The Rosas-linked estates near Camarones and Laguna de los Padres, southern Buenos Aires frontier
juan_manuel_de_rosas.journey.json, for the estanciero network the father worked inside

segments.name: Militia, Defeat, and the First Ink

stops.name: Buenos Aires, enlisted after Caseros
stops.date_confidence: year only: the sources give 1852 for the enlistment without a month, so the entry defaults to 1 January, although the enlistment necessarily follows the battle of 3 February. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate carried across the corpus
stops.campa: Rosas is beaten at Caseros in February and sails for England, and the boy off the frontier ranches comes back to the city and enrols in the militia of the state of Buenos Aires. He is seventeen, a soldier now for the port city he will spend the next twenty years arguing against in print. He was not at Caseros himself; the enlistment can only follow the battle, and no source reached gives it a month. The family has men in both armies: on the other side of that same field his uncle, Colonel Juan José Hernández, was killed fighting for Juan Manuel de Rosas.
suggested_refs: The Caseros battlefield, 3 February 1852, where Colonel Juan José Hernández was killed on the Rosas side

stops.name: Boca del Salado, escaping San Gregorio
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, and rare in naming him personally: the es.wikipedia article on the Combate de San Gregorio lists him among the very few who escaped. It places the fight at the mouth of the Río Salado in the partido de Chascomús and carries no coordinates, so the pin is the town of Chascomús, an approximation. The research pool's geography lens put the site at the San Gregorio near Bolívar, roughly three hundred kilometres west, which is wrong
stops.campa: Hilario Lagos has the city under siege and the province split again. The column Hernández rides with, under Pedro Rosas y Belgrano and Faustino Velazco, is caught at the mouth of the Salado by Gregorio Paz and destroyed on the twenty-second of January. Very few men get out of it. It is the first battle record that names him at all. The chronicle names two of the men who escaped: Colonel Campos, and the young José Hernández, who will one day write Martín Fierro. He is eighteen.
suggested_refs: The Combate de San Gregorio, 22 January 1853, at the mouth of the Río Salado

stops.name: Río Tala, the lieutenancy at El Tala
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested to 8 November 1854. Hernández's presence and his lieutenant's commission rest on biographical tradition and are tagged R: the es.wikipedia article on the Batalla de El Tala does not mention him, and the article on Hilario Lagos dates the action only to early 1854. The pin follows the Río Tala in the partido de San Pedro rather than the town of San Pedro, which the research pool's geography lens used
stops.campa: Manuel Hornos beats Jerónimo Costa and Hilario Lagos near the Río Tala, in the partido de San Pedro, on the eighth of November, and the biographies put Hernández on the winning side of it with a lieutenant's commission. The battle records do not name him. Nobody has produced the commission either. What is certain is that between eighteen and twenty he rides for the port city in three campaigns. He comes out of them with a chest complaint, no money, and a rank that sticks to his name for years whether or not anyone ever granted it.
suggested_refs: The Batalla de El Tala, 8 November 1854, partido de San Pedro

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Reforma Pacífica
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 December 1856 in the Spanish biography. The paper's office address is not located and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate
stops.campa: On the first of December he begins writing for La Reforma Pacífica, and the soldier becomes a journalist without ceasing to be a soldier. He is twenty-two. La Reforma Pacífica speaks for the federal side inside a city that has seceded from the Confederation and means to stay out. It is the trade he keeps for thirty years, through six cities and two exiles; he will found papers of his own and lose them. The pay is bad, the type is set by hand, and an editor who prints the wrong thing in this decade can expect to be closed down, proscribed, or shot at.
suggested_refs: La Reforma Pacífica, Buenos Aires, the federal party paper of the late 1850s

segments.name: Paraná, Capital of a Country That Loses

stops.name: Paraná, the stenographer of the Congress
stops.date_confidence: contested and resolved in favour of the earlier date: es.wikipedia says he was settled in Paraná from 1857, while the research pool's chronology lens carried 1858, which is the year his signed contributions to El Nacional Argentino begin. Year only, defaulted to 1 January. Pin inherited from sarmiento.journey.json, which carries Paraná at the same coordinate
stops.campa: He leaves Buenos Aires for Paraná, capital of the Argentine Confederation, which is the country the port city has seceded from. He works in commerce, then in the public administration, and finally as a stenographer taking down the debates of the Confederation Congress word for word, at speed, in a shorthand nobody else has to be able to read. He does it for four years, having had four years of school in his life. What he takes down is men arguing over what a nation is, at the speed they say it.
suggested_refs: The Congress of the Argentine Confederation at Paraná, 1857 to 1861

stops.name: Cepeda, the Confederation wins
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the battle; Hernández's personal presence is tagged R, since the es.wikipedia article on the Batalla de Cepeda does not name him and no muster roll was reached. Pin inherited byte for byte from julio_argentino_roca.journey.json
stops.campa: Urquiza breaks Mitre's line in the cañada of the arroyo Cepeda, twenty-five kilometres north of Pergamino, and marches on the city. Hernández is with the Confederation, as he is on every field the Confederation fights, and he does not change sides while there is a Confederation to be on the side of. The battle records do not name him, and the biographies put him there without producing an order or a muster roll. Was he in the line at all that day? Nothing reachable says.
suggested_refs: The Cañada de Cepeda battlefield, 23 October 1859

stops.name: Paraná, writing as Vincha
stops.date_confidence: year only for the Vincha articles, defaulted to 1 January; the secretaryship to Vice-President Pedernera is dated 1861 in the same source and is carried in this stop rather than given one of its own
stops.campa: Under the pen name Vincha he writes politics in the Paraná press, and the name has an edge to it: the vincha is the headband a man ties on before a fight. In the same stretch of years he is secretary to Juan Esteban Pedernera, vice-president of the Confederation, and Hernández at twenty-six is close enough to the head of a state to hear it come apart while he files copy about it under a false name. Pedernera holds the presidency for eleven weeks and is the last man to hold it.
suggested_refs: The Vincha articles in the Paraná press, 1860
The vice-presidency and brief presidency of Juan Esteban Pedernera, 1860 to 1861

stops.name: Paraná, the lodge Asilo del Litoral
stops.date_confidence: contested, and the conflict is left open. es.wikipedia gives 28 August 1861 for the initiation, together with Leonidas Echagüe and Teófilo García, with the secretaryship the following year, and the same article's note that shortly before his death in 1886 he was proclaimed a free member for twenty-five years of masonic militancy points arithmetically back to 1861. The research pool's geography lens carried 3 March 1865 from masonic institutional records as the attested date. The earlier date is used here; the lodge minute books would be needed to settle it
stops.campa: He is initiated into the lodge Asilo del Litoral of Paraná on a night in August, with Leonidas Echagüe and Teófilo García, and is its secretary the year after. The Confederation is coming apart; the lodge crosses provincial borders and survives the loss of every battle. Twenty-five years later, weeks from his death, the order proclaims him a free member for a quarter century of militancy, and that arithmetic is the only receipt anybody has for the date. Masonic records give 3 March 1865 instead. The minute books would settle it and nobody has opened them.
suggested_refs: The minute books of the Logia Asilo del Litoral, Paraná, which would settle the 1861 against 1865 initiation date
sources: Research pool, Gran Logia de la Argentina records reported at second hand

stops.name: Pavón, the field abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the battle; Hernández's presence is tagged R, since the es.wikipedia article on the Batalla de Pavón does not name him. Pin inherited byte for byte from julio_argentino_roca.journey.json
stops.campa: Between Rueda and Godoy, forty kilometres south of Rosario, the two armies meet again. Urquiza's cavalry wins its own wing, then rides off the field and goes home, leaving the infantry to Mitre. The Confederation loses a battle it had not lost. Men are left standing in the open while the patron who summoned them rides away, which is the scene Hernández will write for the rest of his life. In thirty years of writing about nearly everything else, he never once described this day in print. No source reached puts him on the field.
suggested_refs: The Pavón battlefield near the Domingo Palacios estancia, 17 September 1861

stops.name: Cañada de Gómez, spared and deserting
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, and one of the very few battle articles that names Hernández directly: the es.wikipedia article on the Batalla de Cañada de Gómez lists him among those spared and notes that he would be the author of Martín Fierro
stops.campa: Two months after Pavón the remnant is surprised at Cañada de Gómez and cut to pieces by Mitrista troops. Hernández is among the men spared, and the survivors are then pressed into the ranks of the army that has just beaten them and marched off to serve it. Levied into a force he did not choose, gone from it the moment the chance comes: that is the plot of the poem he publishes eleven years later. Here it is a field in Santa Fe in November, he is twenty-seven, and he deserts at the first thin guard.
suggested_refs: The Batalla de Cañada de Gómez, 22 November 1861

stops.name: Paraná, El Litoral and the bankruptcy notices
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to 1 January. The syndic advertisements rest on María Celina Ortale's archival study of El Litoral, which the research pool reports but could not fetch directly; carried at reduced confidence pending a check against Ortale's article itself
stops.campa: The Confederation is finished and so is his employment. He writes for El Litoral, Evaristo Carriego's paper in Paraná, and in the same columns runs notices offering his services as a bankruptcy syndic and agent. The advertisement sits on the page beside his own editorials. He has no capital, a marriage a year off, and a trade that pays in instalments. The notices come by way of María Celina Ortale's study of the paper, which the research could not fetch; nobody here has seen one.
suggested_refs: María Celina Ortale's archival study of El Litoral, Paraná, and the Hernández syndic notices
sources: Research pool, reporting Ortale at second hand; the primary article was not reached

stops.name: Paraná, the marriage to Carolina González del Solar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and given identically by es.wikipedia and biografiasyvidas, though the research pool's chronology lens tagged it R. The church or civil registry where the ceremony took place is not named in any source reached
stops.campa: On the eighth of June he marries Carolina González del Solar in Paraná. Eight children are born to them over the next sixteen years, in Paraná and then in Buenos Aires, across two exiles, an armed rising, and the collapse of every political cause he attaches himself to. She keeps a household going through all of it, in cities he is repeatedly thrown out of. Of the private register of that marriage almost nothing survives. No source reached names the church, and none names a witness.
suggested_refs: The eight children of José Hernández and Carolina González del Solar, born between 1865 and 1879

stops.name: Paraná, El Argentino founded
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish biography dates the founding to the middle of 1863 without a day, so the entry defaults to 1 July
stops.campa: He founds his own paper, El Argentino, in the city where the Confederation used to govern. It is the first he owns outright: his name on it, his money in the type, nobody above him to answer to for a line. He is twenty-eight. The founding is dated to the middle of the year and no source reached gives a day for it. Week after week, in Entre Ríos, the paper prints that the state it writes for no longer exists and that the provinces are being brought to order one at a time by the national army.
suggested_refs: El Argentino, Paraná, founded mid-1863

stops.name: Paraná, Rasgos biográficos del general Peñaloza
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month inferred: Ángel Vicente Peñaloza was killed at Olta on 12 November 1863 and the series answering it necessarily follows, so the entry defaults to December. Hernández was not at Olta and is not staged there; the killing is pinned at -30.6167, -66.2667 in sarmiento.journey.json, and appears here only as the subject of a pamphlet written a thousand kilometres away
stops.campa: At Olta in La Rioja national troops kill Ángel Vicente Peñaloza, the Chacho, and set his head on a pike. Sarmiento had written to Mitre two years earlier that there was no need to economise gaucho blood, and the two men will still be arguing over that sentence twelve years from now. Hernández writes the answer: Rasgos biográficos del general D. Ángel V. Peñaloza, later reprinted as Vida del Chacho, which lays the killing at the door of the system Domingo Faustino Sarmiento speaks for. He writes it in Paraná, a thousand kilometres from the body.
suggested_refs: Rasgos biográficos del general D. Ángel V. Peñaloza, Paraná 1863, reissued as Vida del Chacho
The killing of Peñaloza at Olta, 12 November 1863, pinned in sarmiento.journey.json

stops.name: Nogoyá, the convention and the letter to the Chinita
stops.date_confidence: span 1864 to 1865, tagged R and defaulted to mid-1864 to order the segment. The letter opening 'Chinita querida' is dated April 1865 and is reported held by the Biblioteca Pública de las Misiones, which the research could not fetch directly
stops.campa: He serves as secretary to the constitutional convention of Entre Ríos at Nogoyá, taking down another set of debates for another provincial charter. The convention is routine provincial business and left no mark on anything. From there, in April of the following year, he writes his wife a letter, one of the very few surviving pages of him not addressed to a public. The Biblioteca Pública de las Misiones is reported to hold it; the research could not reach the library. It opens: Chinita querida.
suggested_refs: The April 1865 letter to Carolina González del Solar, Biblioteca Pública de las Misiones, Parque del Conocimiento
sources: Research pool, reporting the archive holding at second hand

stops.name: Paysandú, as near as the record puts him
stops.date_confidence: the siege of Paysandú, 2 December 1864 to 2 January 1865, is well documented and its article does not mention Hernández. His proximity to it is disputed among his biographers, no source reached places him inside the town, and the whole item is tagged R
stops.campa: Across the river the Brazilian squadron and Venancio Flores are grinding down Leandro Gómez and the blanco garrison of Paysandú. Thirty-three days of bombardment. The town falls on the second of January and Gómez is taken out and shot. Hernández moves toward the siege while it is still going on. Whether he reached it, whether he fought in it, or whether he got as far as the far bank and stood there watching the smoke come off the roofs, the biographies do not agree and the documents do not say.
suggested_refs: The Sitio de Paysandú, 2 December 1864 to 2 January 1865
sources: Research pool, biographical tradition, tagged R

stops.name: Corrientes, fiscal to Evaristo López
stops.date_confidence: span 1865 to May 1868, defaulted to the first year. His exact title in López's administration is given variously as interim fiscal of the state, secretary, and minister-general, and the sources do not resolve it
stops.campa: In Corrientes he takes office under Governor Evaristo López, named interim fiscal of the state, and teaches grammar at the Colegio San Agustín to make the salary reach. The province is a rear area of the Paraguayan war and a federal government inside a country run by its enemies. He holds the post three years. In May of 1868 a Mitrista rising deposes López, and Hernández is out of office and out of the province. What his title actually was, the sources give three ways: interim fiscal, secretary, minister-general.
suggested_refs: The administration of Governor Evaristo López of Corrientes, deposed May 1868
The Colegio San Agustín, Corrientes

stops.name: Corrientes, El Eco and the war upriver
stops.date_confidence: span 1866 to 1868 for his work at El Eco de Corrientes, defaulted to the first year. Hernández was not present at Curupayty; that battle is pinned at -27.1131, -58.5744 in julio_argentino_roca.journey.json and appears here only as what his journalism was written against
stops.campa: He writes for El Eco de Corrientes against the war and against Bartolomé Mitre's conduct of it, from a province that supplies the conscripts and buries them. The first great quarrel of his life was over Peñaloza; this one is with the man governing the country. Mitre is president while he writes it, and the province is one that government means to take back. A short way upriver the allied armies walk into the trenches at Curupayty behind a bombardment that has not touched them, and lose four thousand men in an afternoon.
suggested_refs: El Eco de Corrientes, 1866 to 1868
The Curupayty earthworks, 22 September 1866, pinned in julio_argentino_roca.journey.json

stops.name: Rosario, La Capital and the capital question
stops.date_confidence: attested: his articles in La Capital run from 20 June to 21 July 1868, signed J. H.
stops.campa: Ovidio Lagos brings him to Rosario for a month at La Capital, where he signs himself J. H., defends provincial legality, and argues that the national capital belongs on the Paraná at Rosario rather than at the port of Buenos Aires. It is a proposal with a long life ahead of it and no future. He is thirty-three, has just been thrown out of one province, and is writing in another man's paper. The articles run from the twentieth of June to the twenty-first of July and then stop.
suggested_refs: The J. H. articles in La Capital, Rosario, 20 June to 21 July 1868

segments.name: El Río de la Plata, Victoria 202

stops.name: Victoria 202, the paper of municipal autonomy
stops.date_confidence: the address is attested, Victoria 202, today Hipólito Yrigoyen 202 between Defensa and Bolívar; the founding date is not established, and the research pool's own two lenses give 1868 and 1869. Year defaulted to 1 January 1869. The pin follows the street address and corrects the pool's geography lens, which sat five hundred metres west near Perú and Chacabuco
stops.campa: He installs the administration and editorial rooms of El Río de la Plata at Victoria 202, a few blocks from the government house, and for something over a year runs the most serious paper he will ever run. It campaigns for municipal autonomy, for the popular election of local officials, against the arbitrary frontier levy that empties the countryside of men, and for Argentine sovereignty over the Malvinas. The argument of Martín Fierro is already here, three years early, in prose and signed with his name. The Malvinas plank is the one reported at second hand; no issue carrying those editorials was reached.
suggested_refs: El Río de la Plata, Victoria 202, Buenos Aires, 1869 to 1870

stops.name: Victoria 202, the editorial on the Indians
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the verbatim excerpt is reproduced by elhistoriador.com.ar in an article whose title promises a Malvinas quotation and whose body quotes this passage on Indigenous policy instead. The original issue of the paper was not consulted
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of August the paper prints a sentence the next decade of Argentine history runs straight over: that the country has no right to expel the Indians from the territory, and still less to exterminate them. The line is not an aside. The paper carries the frontier week after week, the levy, the forts, the wagons, the treaties made and dropped. Ten years later the army crosses the Río Negro and does precisely what the sentence says it may not do. The editorial is signed and dated and sits in the file.
stops.quote: Nosotros no tenemos el derecho de expulsar a los indios del territorio y menos de exterminarlos...
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, editorial in El Río de la Plata, Buenos Aires, 19 August 1869, as quoted by elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The El Río de la Plata editorial of 19 August 1869 on frontier and Indigenous policy
sources: elhistoriador.com.ar, 'José Hernández y la soberanía de Malvinas'

stops.name: Victoria 202, closed on the news from San José
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; es.wikipedia states plainly that the paper was closed on 22 April 1870 by Hernández himself, after the assassination of Urquiza. Urquiza was killed at the Palacio San José on 11 April 1870; that site is not pinned here, because Hernández was not there
stops.campa: On the eleventh of April Justo José de Urquiza is shot in his own palace at San José by men of López Jordán's faction. On the twenty-second, Hernández closes El Río de la Plata himself. No censor shuts it and no creditor forecloses on it; the paper is a year and some months old and is not failing. The editor decides that what is now coming cannot be argued out in a newspaper office in Buenos Aires. He stops the presses sixteen months after he started them, on a morning, by himself.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Justo José de Urquiza at the Palacio San José, Entre Ríos, 11 April 1870

segments.name: The Rising, the Border, and the Poem

stops.name: Paraná, joining López Jordán
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month inferred to order the segment. His movements inside Entre Ríos during the rising are not located in any source reached, so the pin is the provincial capital as the nearest fixed point, not a claim about where he was
stops.campa: Ricardo López Jordán has raised Entre Ríos against the national government, and Hernández goes to him as adviser and propagandist and, one more time, as a man on the losing side by choice. He has spent eighteen months arguing in print that the countryside is being governed by force and that force is not government. The argument has run out of newspapers. He is thirty-five, with a wife and small children back in Buenos Aires, and the rising has six months to live. Where he went inside Entre Ríos, and what he did there, no source reached says.
suggested_refs: The first Jordanist rebellion in Entre Ríos, 1870 to 1871

stops.name: Ñaembé, the rebellion broken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, and the es.wikipedia article on the Batalla de Ñaembé names Hernández among López Jordán's companions on the field. The pin is inherited byte for byte from julio_argentino_roca.journey.json, which carries the same battle; the site at Colonia Carolina near Goya would geocode nearer -29.14, -59.27
stops.campa: At the Ñaembé stream near Goya the national army runs the rising down and finishes it. Among López Jordán's companions on the field is the writer José Hernández. Among the officers who break them is Julio Argentino Roca, twenty-eight years old, made colonel that same day for his part in it. In ten years Roca will be president and Hernández a senator voting for his capital. For now the rising is finished, and Hernández rides north for the border with nothing.
suggested_refs: The Ñaembé battlefield at Colonia Carolina near Goya, Corrientes, 26 January 1871

stops.name: Santana do Livramento, the first exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1871 through the beginning of 1872 in the Spanish biography; the month is given, the day is defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He crosses into Brazil and sits out the year at Santana do Livramento, a town on the line where Rio Grande do Sul becomes Uruguay and neither country is his. He is thirty-six, proscribed, and unemployable in three provinces. It is the first of his two exiles and the shorter one. He writes home, and those letters are kept. The border runs down the middle of the street there, and a man standing on one kerb is out of reach of the government on the other.
suggested_refs: The exile letters sent home from Santana do Livramento, 1871 to 1872, held at the Chacra Pueyrredón museum

stops.name: Gran Hotel Argentino, the poem written at a hotel table
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the composition, month inferred to order the segment. The hotel is named in the Spanish biography in connection with the writing; the picturesque detail that he wrote on butcher's wrapping paper or in a pulpería ledger is folklore, tagged R, and no manuscript or hotel register was reached either to confirm or to refute it. The hotel's exact address is not located and the pin is an approximation near the Plaza de Mayo, consistent with 'almost opposite the government house'
stops.campa: Back in Buenos Aires and still politically exposed, he takes a room at the Gran Hotel Argentino, almost opposite the government house, and there, by his own later account, writes to keep off the tedium of hotel life. Tradition adds butcher's paper and a pulpería ledger, neither of which anyone has ever produced. What he has is thirty-seven years of frontier, militia, defeat, office and print, and a six-line stanza he did not invent. He is writing it out in a rented room, across the square from the government that has twice proscribed him.
stops.quote: Querido amigo: Al fin me he decidido a que mi pobre Martín Fierro, que me ha ayudado algunos momentos a alejar el fastidio de la vida del Hotel, salga a conocer el mundo, y allá va acogido al amparo de su nombre.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, dedicatory letter to José Zoilo Miguens, El gaucho Martín Fierro (Buenos Aires, December 1872)
suggested_refs: The Gran Hotel Argentino, Buenos Aires, and the composition tradition of 1872
sources: El gaucho Martín Fierro, dedicatory letter, consulted in the Internet Archive text of the fifteenth edition, 1894

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La República begins printing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the first instalments in La República; the book followed from the press of La Pampa in December. The specific press addresses are not located and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of November the newspaper La República begins printing El gaucho Martín Fierro in instalments, and in December the book follows from the press of La Pampa, with a letter to José Zoilo Miguens in front of it. It is a poem about a man taken by the levy, ruined, and turned outlaw, in the metre and the vocabulary of the men it is about. It sells in bookshops and in pulperías, where it is read out loud to men who cannot read it themselves. Within six years there are eleven editions.
stops.quote: Aquí me pongo a cantar / Al compás de la vigüela, / Que el hombre que lo desvela / Una pena extraordinaria, / Como la ave solitaria / Con el cantar se consuela.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, El gaucho Martín Fierro, Canto I, opening sextet (Buenos Aires, 1872)
suggested_refs: The first edition of El gaucho Martín Fierro, Imprenta de La Pampa, Buenos Aires, December 1872
Leopoldo Lugones's 1913 lectures at the Teatro Odeón, published 1916 as El payador, which recast the poem as national epic
Jorge Luis Borges and Margarita Guerrero, El 'Martín Fierro' (1953), a later reading of the poem against its epic-nationalist canonization

stops.name: Montevideo, La Patria and El Patagón
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 November 1873 for the resumption of work at La Patria; the nine El Patagón articles answering Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna are dated 1874. The paper's office address is not located and the pin is the Montevideo city centre
stops.campa: The second Jordanist rising sends him across the river again. In Montevideo he writes for and then directs La Patria alongside Héctor Soto, and in 1874 produces the nine articles signed El Patagón, answering the Chilean Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna over the southern territories. He is forty, in his second exile, running a foreign newspaper while the book he wrote in a hotel room two years ago outsells everything ever printed in Argentina. He starts at La Patria on the first of November.
suggested_refs: The nine El Patagón articles, La Patria, Montevideo, 1874

stops.name: Montevideo, the paper closes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 January 1875 for the closure of La Patria; the date of his own crossing back to Buenos Aires under Avellaneda's conciliation policy is not separately given
stops.campa: La Patria stops on the first day of the year and the second exile ends with it. Nicolás Avellaneda is president and his policy is conciliation: the men proscribed after 1870 may come home, and the ones who took up arms against the state are to be counted as citizens again. Hernández comes home, though the date of his own crossing back is not recorded anywhere reached. He is forty and has been in and out of Buenos Aires for eighteen years, on the beaten side of four wars. He lives in the city for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The conciliation policy of President Nicolás Avellaneda, 1874 onward

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Señor Sarmiento: ¿por qué mataron?
stops.date_confidence: September 1875 per the research pool's chronology; the day is not given and defaults to the first. The office of Manuel Bilbao's La Libertad is not located and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate
stops.campa: A new edition of Vida del Chacho brings La Tribuna down on him, and he answers in Manuel Bilbao's La Libertad. The pamphlet that started it is selling again. Twelve years have passed since Olta; Domingo Faustino Sarmiento has been president of the republic in the interval and is a senator now, and neither man has moved a step from where he stood in 1863. The title of the article is a question addressed to Sarmiento by name: Señor Sarmiento, por qué mataron?
suggested_refs: 'Señor Sarmiento: por qué mataron?', La Libertad, Buenos Aires, September 1875

stops.name: Tacuarí 17, the Librería del Plata
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the partnership with Rafael Casagemas to 1878 and says he had bought the shop outright by the end of that year; no day is given and the entry defaults to 1 January. The pin is a geocode of Tacuarí 17, Monserrat, and corrects the research pool's geography lens by some six hundred metres
stops.campa: In partnership with Rafael Casagemas he sets up the Librería del Plata at Tacuarí 17, and by the end of the year he has bought the whole of it. The author of the best-selling book in the country now controls a counter, a shelf, and a route by which books reach the interior. He is his own agent. Two years ago five thousand copies were printed and knowing men said the run would hold for half a century; he does the arithmetic himself in the front of the eleventh edition.
stops.quote: Cuando hace dos años se anunció un tiraje de 5000 ejemplares del Martín Fierro, los que no saben apreciar la boga y popularidad de este poema, vaticinaron que con este número habría para medio siglo. Empero, semejante cálculo ha resultado tan erróneo que es ya necesario precipitar una reimpresión porque no se encuentra un solo ejemplar en las librerías.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, letter to the editors prefacing the eleventh edition of Martín Fierro, 1878, quoted in María Celina Ortale, 'El archivo José Hernández y las Obras Completas' (UNLP-FaHCE, 2021)
suggested_refs: The Librería del Plata, Tacuarí 17, Buenos Aires, from 1878
sources: María Celina Ortale, 'El archivo José Hernández y las Obras Completas', in Las lenguas del archivo (UNLP-FaHCE, 2021)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La vuelta de Martín Fierro
stops.date_confidence: year attested, no day given, defaulted to 1 January. First edition Pablo E. Coni, Buenos Aires, 1879, illustrated by Carlos Clérice
stops.campa: Seven years after the first part he brings the gaucho back, and the man who returns is not the man who rode out. Fierro sings a payada with a black singer about time and the weight of the world, gives his sons their advice, and tells them to scatter and change their names. Pablo E. Coni prints it and Carlos Clérice draws the plates. The first printing is twenty thousand copies, a figure that comes from Hernández's own prologue and from no printer's record anyone has produced. In the same year the army crosses the Río Negro.
stops.quote: Los hermanos sean unidos, / Porque esa es la ley primera
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, La vuelta de Martín Fierro (Buenos Aires: Pablo E. Coni, 1879), canto XXXII, the consejos to his sons; verified on the Wikisource transcription of the Academia Argentina de Letras first-edition scan
suggested_refs: La vuelta de Martín Fierro, Pablo E. Coni, Buenos Aires 1879, illustrated by Carlos Clérice
Leopoldo Lugones's El payador (1916), which made the two parts into a national epic
Jorge Luis Borges and Margarita Guerrero, El 'Martín Fierro' (1953)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the lodge Obediencia a la Ley
stops.date_confidence: 30 December 1879 per masonic institutional records reported at second hand in the research pool and not independently re-fetched; tagged R. The senior offices, First Grand Warden in 1880 and 1881, rest on the same chain. The lodge's meeting address is not located and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of December he joins the Buenos Aires lodge Obediencia a la Ley, eighteen years after the initiation at Paraná. Masonic sources put him in senior office the following year, First Grand Warden for 1880 and 1881, though the minute books behind that claim were not reached. He is a bookseller, a provincial legislator and the author of a sequel that has just sold twenty thousand copies, and now a mason in the capital as well, with four sets of doors open at once.
suggested_refs: The records of the Logia Obediencia a la Ley No. 13, Buenos Aires
sources: Research pool, Gran Logia de la Argentina and masoneria-argentina.org.ar, reported at second hand

segments.name: The Senate, the Quinta, and the Day of Tradition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the senate and the federalization
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month inferred to order the segment. Two corrections to the research pool: es.wikipedia places the federalization debate in the provincial senate, not in the chamber of deputies, and nothing reached supports the pool's claim that Hernández presided over the chamber. The legislature's building is not identified and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate
stops.campa: In the provincial senate he defends the federalization of the city of Buenos Aires against Leandro N. Alem, who warns the chamber about gathering the whole power of the nation into one place. Hernández has spent his life against the port city: at Cepeda, at Pavón, at Ñaembé, and in Rosario arguing that the capital belonged on the Paraná. The Confederation lost its war, and he has decided the country needs a head more than he needs to be right. He votes to make Buenos Aires the capital.
suggested_refs: The 1880 federalization debate in the Buenos Aires provincial senate, Hernández against Leandro N. Alem

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Instrucción del estanciero
stops.date_confidence: contested and left open: es.wikipedia dates the Instrucción del estanciero to 1881 and biografiasyvidas to 1882. The earlier date is used and the discrepancy is not resolved. No day is given and the entry defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: He publishes the Instrucción del estanciero, a practical manual for ranch owners: stock, land, fencing, wages, and the handling of the men who do the work. The hand that gave Martín Fierro his complaint against the estancia now writes the estancia's handbook. He sees no contradiction in it and says as much in the preface. The countryside he wants is one where the work is paid and the levy is gone, and the owner is the man he has decided can be argued into building it. One biography dates the book to 1881 and another to 1882.
suggested_refs: Instrucción del estanciero, Buenos Aires, 1881 or 1882

stops.name: La Plata, the name of the city
stops.date_confidence: the founding of La Plata on 19 November 1882 is attested. Hernández's collaboration with Dardo Rocha and the claim that he devised the name are stated directly in the es.wikipedia article on Hernández and are absent from the article on the city, which credits Rocha alone; the attribution is contested and tagged R. The research pool's geography lens wrongly concluded the claim was unsourced after checking only the city article
stops.campa: Dardo Rocha lays out a new provincial capital on open ground below Buenos Aires, a grid with diagonals cut across it, and Hernández is one of the men working on the project. His own biographical record says the name of the city was his idea. The city's own record credits Rocha and mentions nobody else. Both accounts were printed long after both men were dead. He is a senator of the province the city is being built to govern. A locality of its partido carries his name.
suggested_refs: The founding of La Plata by Dardo Rocha, 19 November 1882
The locality of José Hernández, partido de La Plata
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'La Plata', which does not mention him

stops.name: Buenos Aires, fifty-eight thousand copies
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the twelfth edition, the last published in his lifetime; no day is given and the entry defaults to 1 January. The capitals in the quoted notice are Hernández's own emphasis per Ortale
stops.campa: The twelfth edition, ten thousand copies, brings the running total to fifty-eight thousand, and he writes the publisher's notice himself, in capital letters. Nothing printed in the country has done anything like it, and he says so in the tone of a man reading out a return of stock. He is forty-eight, a senator and a bookseller. The notice is known here because María Celina Ortale transcribed it out of the archive; no copy of the edition itself was handled. It is the last one to appear in his lifetime and the last thing about the poem he ever signs.
stops.quote: Al ofrecer al público, esta vez, la duodécima edición de la 'Ida y Vuelta de Martín Fierro', creemos de estricta justicia consagrar algunas palabras al más extraordinario triunfo de publicidad que registran nuestros anales bibliográficos. La presente edición de diez mil ejemplares viene a integrar la asombrosa cifra de CINCUENTA Y OCHO MIL: hecho sin precedente en estos países americanos, y muy raro también en los Estados Europeos de origen latino.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, 'Advertencia Editorial' to the twelfth edition of Martín Fierro, 1883, quoted in María Celina Ortale, 'El archivo José Hernández y las Obras Completas' (UNLP-FaHCE, 2021), p. 169 n. 1
suggested_refs: The twelfth edition of the Ida y Vuelta de Martín Fierro, 1883, the last in the author's lifetime
sources: María Celina Ortale, 'El archivo José Hernández y las Obras Completas', in Las lenguas del archivo (UNLP-FaHCE, 2021)

stops.name: Avenida Cabildo 468, the quinta at Belgrano
stops.date_confidence: attested to Thursday 21 October 1886, death by myocarditis leading to cardiac arrest, at fifty-one. The pin is a geocode of the address the Spanish biography itself gives, the then Santa Fe street, now Avenida Cabildo, number 468, and corrects the research pool's placement at the Belgrano neighbourhood centre by roughly two kilometres. The reported last words are deathbed tradition, tagged R, with no contemporaneous bedside account behind them
stops.campa: He dies at his quinta in Belgrano, then still a municipality of its own on the northern edge of the city, of a myocarditis that stops his heart. It is a Thursday, the twenty-first of October, and he is fifty-one. The house stands on what is then Santa Fe street and is now Avenida Cabildo, at number 468, a number local historians dispute. He fought the port city at Cepeda, at Pavón and at Ñaembé, and he dies inside it. Nobody at the bedside wrote anything down at the time, and every biography since has repeated what the family says he said: Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Hernández quinta at Santa Fe 468, now Avenida Cabildo 468, Belgrano

stops.name: Recoleta, the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial in the Cementerio de la Recoleta is attested; no day is given in the sources reached and the entry defaults to the day after the death. The pin is the coordinate already carried for the Recoleta in sarmiento.journey.json; juan_manuel_de_rosas.journey.json carries the same cemetery nine ten-thousandths of a degree east, and the research pool's afterlife lens gave a third value
stops.campa: They bury him in the Recoleta, in the few hectares of ground where unitarios and federales end up together regardless of which of them won. He is fifty-one years old, dead a day, and a sitting senator of the province. The book is in its twelfth edition and there is not a copy of it left in the shops. His plot and section are not identified in any source reached, and the cemetery's own list of notable burials does not name him among its featured dead.
suggested_refs: The Cementerio de la Recoleta, Junín 1760, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Chacra de Perdriel, the tenth of November
stops.date_confidence: posthumous stop at the birth pin, dated to the earliest of the acts it carries. Buenos Aires provincial law 4756 of 1939 established the Día de la Tradición on his birthday; national law 21.154 of 1975 made the observance binding nationally. The chacra was bequeathed for a museum in 1959 by Elvira Zulema Lynch Pueyrredón de Lynch, the donation accepted by decree 11.524 of 17 December 1965, the museum constituted by decree 3570 of 28 October 1966, and the site declared a National Historical Monument in 1972
stops.campa: Fifty-three years after his death the province makes his birthday the Día de la Tradición, and in 1975 the nation follows. The room he was born in is left for a museum in 1959, constituted by decree in 1966, and declared a national monument in 1972. A poem written against the conscription of gauchos is now the document of national character, taught in schools and printed by the state. In the room at Perdriel, in a case, are the letters he sent home from Brazil in the year he had lost everything.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires provincial law 4756 of 1939 and national law 21.154 of 1975, establishing the Día de la Tradición
The Museo Histórico José Hernández, Chacra Pueyrredón, partido de General San Martín
sources: argentina.gob.ar, 'José Hernández y el Día de la Tradición'
